articles.title: Instead of continuing war, Azerbaijan has chosen path of lasting peace with Armenia: Hikmet Hajiyev - 1Lurer
articles.summary: Instead of continuing war, Azerbaijan has chosen path of lasting peace with Armenia: Hikmet Hajiyev  1Lurer
articles.full_text:
Azerbaijani Presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev has discussed the peace process with Armenia during a conversation with American economist and professor Jeffrey Sachs in Baku.
Hajiyev spoke about bilateral trade relations, the development of transport links, and opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy.
He said Baku also views the peace process in the context of transforming the South Caucasus into a platform for cooperation.
“In our bilateral relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan, we are also putting the historical past aside. There are still unhealed wounds and memories that we cannot turn a blind eye to. At the same time, however, we are looking toward the future, toward lasting peace. Trade relations between the two countries have already begun. We are building links and developing connectivity,” Hajiyev said.
The Azerbaijani presidential aide said that Armenia is being offered the opportunity to join the region’s connectivity network.
“Armenia is a landlocked country. We are offering Armenia the opportunity to become a country connected to our region’s connectivity network, providing it with various opportunities to develop transport links,” he said.
Speaking about energy cooperation, Hajiyev said Azerbaijan plans to increase its renewable electricity generation capacity in the coming years. According to him, the country plans to have an additional 2 gigawatts of capacity in the coming years, followed by an additional 8 gigawatts of capacity ready for export.
Hajiyev said Baku also views these plans in the context of peacebuilding with Armenia.
“Now the war is over, and we are trying to present the economic benefits of the concept of peace, as well as the concept of green energy – the peace dividend. We hope that green energy will become one of the components of this strategy, including along the Caspian Sea,” he said.

Russian media said the call covered topics including the Ukraine war and specifically a local ceasefire in Oleshky, which began on Tuesday morning.
Finnish president Alexander Stubb defended holding talks with Ukraine’s aggressor, saying “ending the war requires direct discussions”. Recap: Finnish and Norwegian leaders hold rare call with Putin to urge end to Ukraine war
04:00 , Shweta Sharma
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held rare direct calls with Russian president Vladimir Putin, urging him to end the war in Ukraine as diplomatic efforts gain momentum ahead of fresh peace negotiations.
Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere spoke to Putin for around 90 minutes on Tuesday before holding a separate conversation with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky.
The call marked a significant departure from the approach taken by most Western European leaders, who have largely avoided direct contact with the Kremlin since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
“The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said.
Stoere said he and Stubb had "stressed the importance of de-escalation." Both voiced strong support for Ukraine.
The two leaders said the initiative was linked to planned peace talks between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi next month.
However, the Kremlin showed no indication of softening its demands, insisting that any lasting peace must fully take Russia's interests into account.
The diplomatic outreach also exposed divisions among European leaders, with Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen warning against countries acting alone and Sweden's Ulf Kristersson expressing little hope of a breakthrough.
Ukraine welcomed the initiative, saying the talks had been coordinated with Kyiv.

Zelensky, speaking in his nightly video address, cited a report by senior commanders to say that, for the first time, the "Veles" operation used pipelines in Ukraine's northeast.
He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the "Vivaldi" operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but which has been under constant Russian pressure.
"It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions," Zelensky said.
"Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success," he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine's Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kms (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused on the north of the key strongholds in the region, the so-called "fortress belt" of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.

Russia and Ukraine continued observing a limited ceasefire in occupied Kherson Oblast on October 28, but it remains unclear whether Ukrainian civilians will have a legitimate and duress-free choice to return to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova confirmed on October 28 that there were no ceasefire violations in Russian-occupied Oleshky in the first 30 hours since the agreement entered into force on the morning of October 27.
[1] US First Lady Melania Trump reported on October 27 that the limited ceasefire will cover other unspecified areas of Kherson Oblast to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys, and sources told the BBC on October 27 that the ceasefire extends to all of Kherson Oblast.
[2] Fox News published on October 28 reported photos of the ceasefire agreement confirming that the Ukrainian delegation and Oleshky residents who wish to evacuate to Ukraine will travel to Anapa, Krasnodar Krai in Russia and then to Gomel, Belarus on October 31.
[3] The part of the agreement that Fox News reported did not provide details on how the evacuated Oleshky citizens and the Ukrainian delegation will subsequently travel from Belarus to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine, however.
The photos of the ceasefire agreement indicate that the Russian Dnepr Grouping of Forces (GoF) is facilitating the ceasefire.
Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov inspected the Russian Dnepr GoF and met with its commander, Colonel General Mikhail Teplinsky, on October 27, and the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that they primarily discussed Russian unmanned system operations in the area.
[4] Russian forces may use the limited ceasefire to reconstitute their forces in Kherson Oblast.
It remains unclear how Russian authorities will treat Ukrainians evacuated from Oleshky and whether Russian authorities will provide the residents a legitimate and duress-free choice to return to Ukrainian government-controlled Ukraine.
[5]
The Kremlin continues efforts to persuade the Trump administration to make economic concessions and pursue business cooperation with Russia, even as Russia continues to refuse to make any concessions of its own to end its war in Ukraine.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed on October 27 that the October 9 US-Russia diesel deal is a “purely business agreement” and that there were “no conditions or stipulations whatsoever” requiring any Russian political action or security concerns in exchange for the US purchase of Russian diesel.
[6] Lavrov also noted that the informational war around Ukraine will continue and even has a “tendency to escalate.
” Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov similarly claimed on October 13 that there is “no direct connection” between the US-Russia diesel deal and peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
[7] Lavrov’s and Peskov’s statements notably contradict Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev’s October 12 claim that the diesel deal facilitates efforts for peace in Ukraine and Dmitriev’s October 17 claim that the suspension of some US sanctions on Russia would facilitate a “lasting peace” in Ukraine.
[8] High-ranking Kremlin officials are attempting to separate economic agreements with the United States from peace negotiations in order to obtain US economic concessions that will support Russia’s continued war effort while Russia has made no concessions that would enable any meaningful peace negotiations.
[9] Kremlin officials have repeatedly affirmed Russia’s commitment to its long-standing maximalist military goals in Ukraine and refusal to make any concessions toward a peace settlement.
[10]
Kremlin officials continue attempts to exclude Europe from peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine while reiterating Russia’s 2021 demand for NATO to rollback its presence in Europe.
Lavrov claimed that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s October 27 call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store demonstrated the European desire to “squeeze” themselves into peace negotiations.
[11] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov claimed on October 28 that Russia, Ukraine, and the United States do not plan to have European representatives at the planned trilateral peace negotiations in November.
[12] Peskov, however, claimed on October 25 that Russian would support a European peace negotiator, especially one who wants to facilitate a peace settlement.
[13] Peskov’s statement suggests that Russia will only support European negotiators who will surrender to Russia’s maximalist demands for full Ukrainian capitulation.
Lavrov’s and Ushakov’s statements came against the backdrop of the Kremlin’s recent renewal of the demands it first articulated in December 2021 that included retrograding the membership of NATO states that joined the alliance since 1997 — effectively granting Russia a veto over NATO internal policies and curtailing the sovereignty of many European states to choose to join alliances.
[14] The Kremlin has routinely tried to exclude European leaders from peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, including portraying the United States and Russia as the only relevant negotiating actors.
[15]
Three unidentified — possibly Russian — unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) struck a cargo ship off the coast of Bulgaria on October 28. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov stated on October 28 that three USVs struck the Contship Jet container ship approximately “21 miles” (likely referring to nautical miles) southeast of Shalba, Bulgaria.[16] Automatic identification systems (AIS) data from Marine Traffic, a shipping tracking website, indicates that the Liberian-flagged Contship Jet ship was traveling from Haifa, Israel to Constanta, Romania, and Greek shipping company Contships Management stated that the vessel’s crew included four Ukrainians.[17] A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed that the Contship Jet could have been carrying unspecified cargo to Constanta, a supply hub for Ukraine.[18] The October 28 strike comes against the backdrop of recent Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including drone strikes against civilian vessels near and within Romanian territorial waters on October 13, 14, and 23 and within the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on October 5 and overnight on October 12 to 13.[19]
Russia continues to actively support Iranian-backed operations against US allies in the Middle East.
[NOTE: A version of the following text also appeared in ISW-CTP’s October 28 Iran Update.
] A Switzerland-based geospatial intelligence firm told the Associated Press on October 28 that it has consistently observed Russian military satellites positioned above major Saudi energy and military sites in the days prior to and following Houthi drone and missile strikes against Saudi Arabia.
[20] Russian satellite activity followed a similar pattern around strikes against Saudi infrastructure originating from Iraq, where the Houthis maintain a presence.
A Saudi official and a high-ranking Houthi official separately told the Associated Press that Russia is providing satellite-based targeting intelligence to the Houthis, reportedly through Iranian military advisers who are operating in Yemen.
[21] Russian pre- and post-strike imagery very likely enables the Houthis and Iranian military advisers to conduct battle damage assessments of their strikes.
[22] The geospatial intelligence firm observed 40 instances of Russian satellite positioning over Saudi military and energy sites between July 1 and October 19, including the September 10 drone strike on the Saudi East-West Pipeline.
[23] Russian support is enabling the Iranian-supported Houthi campaign to constrain Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil during a global energy crisis that Iran has caused by striking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
[24]
Russian support for Houthi efforts to disrupt Saudi energy exports is consistent with long-standing Russian support for Iran and its regional partners, particularly the Houthis. Russia previously provided the Houthis with satellite-based targeting intelligence to help the group strike US vessels and international shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in 2023 and 2024, for example.[25] The Houthis supported Russia, in turn, by promising to not target Russian vessels in the Red Sea and by recruiting Yemenis to fight for Russia in Ukraine.[26] Russia has also provided targeting intelligence to support Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia and other regional targets during the current conflict in the Middle East, according to unspecified sources speaking to the Associated Press.[27] Russian intelligence sharing with Iran and its partners in the ongoing war demonstrates how Russia is directly supporting Iranian and Iranian-backed efforts to disrupt global energy markets and raise the cost of oil.[28]

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. Uzbekistan is seeking to strengthen trade, investment and transport links between Europe, Central Asia and China through new business partnerships, following an international business forum organized by the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade in cooperation with Vienna-based Global Neighbours in Tashkent on October 27.
This was stated by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, following a meeting between Deputy Minister Ilzat Kasimov, Global Neighbours Founder and Chairwoman Jovanka Porsche, and representatives of the business community and expert circles.
The discussions focused on Uzbekistan’s investment potential, ongoing economic reforms and opportunities to develop joint initiatives connecting the three regions.
Participants also explored industrial cooperation, transport infrastructure, the digital economy and innovation as potential areas for expanding cross-border business ties.
The program included a thematic roundtable, as well as business-to-business (B2B) and government-to-business (G2B) meetings designed to establish direct contacts between companies, investors and government representatives.
The meetings provided a platform for participants to discuss potential projects, identify areas of mutual interest and explore opportunities for practical cooperation.
Global Neighbours is a Vienna-based international think tank founded in 2022 by entrepreneur Jovanka Porsche, together with former Austrian Chancellor Christian Kern and former German Vice Chancellor Philipp Rösler. The organization focuses on fostering dialogue and cooperation between Europe and Asia, bringing together representatives of business, politics and expert communities to explore cross-border partnerships.

Resulting from its concerted effort to increase cooperation and interdependence with its neighbors, Turkey saw an expansion in its soft power in the Middle East. As tensions rose throughout the Middle East, Turkey found itself increasingly involved in the region’s affairs. Its involvement was often at odds with Russian interests, however, leading to uneasy relations with its regional neighbor.
Turkish involvement in the Arab Spring and the Syrian Civil War
Although Turkey had become increasingly confrontational by the close of the new millennium’s first decade, it was the onset of the Arab Spring that ultimately unraveled Turkey’s commitment to peaceful diplomacy. The wave of Arab Spring uprisings in 2011–12 destabilized several Middle Eastern countries that had been on friendly terms with Turkey, requiring an initially hesitant Turkish government to take sides. As the uprisings toppled Tunisian Pres. Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali and Egyptian Pres. Hosni Mubarak and the end of Libyan leader Muammar al-Qaddafi’s rule appeared imminent, Turkey began proactively supporting the democratic movements taking hold across the Middle East.
Its support extended to the democratic movement in Syria, despite the movement taking aim against Erdoğan’s close ally, Syrian Pres. Bashar al-Assad. As the regime’s response to the uprising escalated, Turkey provided safe haven for the opposition and began providing military and financial support to the Russia, meanwhile, offered support to the Assad regime, helping to prop up an ally critical to Russian interests in the Middle East. Foreign involvement on either side of the uprising lent fuel to a full-fledged civil war.
By mid-2016 Turkey’s southern border with Syria was threatened by the rise of militants of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS) as well as emboldened Kurdish separatists, prompting a Turkish offensive into northwestern Syria that lasted until March 2017. Turkish forces remained in northern Syria, however, to maintain a buffer zone and protect Syrian rebels there. The following year Assad’s forces swept through rebel-held territories in the country’s southwest and left the Turkish-occupied northwest as the rebels’ only haven. A brutal conflict to retake the northwest was anticipated but was ultimately staved off through the cooperative efforts of Turkey and Russia to prevent it. In October 2019 Turkey launched an offensive to subdue Kurdish separatists along its border in northeastern Syria; a temporary ceasefire negotiated by the United States days later was made permanent after Russian mediation arranged a 30-km (18-mile) buffer zone along the Turkish border.
Although Turkey had largely steered clear of direct confrontation with Syrian government forces, Turkish forces in February 2020 retaliated directly against Syrian troops after dozens of Turkish soldiers were killed in an air strike. The confrontation ended, however, after a general ceasefire was negotiated by Turkey and Russia the following week. The ceasefire largely brought hostilities to an end until 2024, although Turkish forces remained in northern Syria. The Turkish government also fostered a cooperative relationship with Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a rebel group—designated a terrorist organization by Turkey and unaffiliated with the Turkish-backed opposition—that had managed to stave off the advance of government forces in the bordering governorate of Idlib and had asserted autonomy there since 2017. In November 2024 hostilities in the civil war were reignited when HTS launched an offensive against the Syrian regime, leading to its downfall in less than two weeks’ time.
Turkish intervention in the Libyan Civil War
Meanwhile, Turkey deployed troops to Libya in January 2020 to support the internationally recognized government based in Tripoli. There, as in Syria, Turkish intervention stood against that of Russia, which backed the opposition government based in Tobruk. Nevertheless, the intervention broke a yearlong stalemate in the country’s civil war and forced opposition fighters to retreat hundreds of miles before a ceasefire was announced in August. The ceasefire led to a period of rapprochement in Libya and an attempt at unity government that lasted through most of 2021.
Turkey’s interest in Libya extended beyond merely influencing the outcome of the war, however. Its intervention was predicated on a 2019 maritime agreement with the government in Tripoli to create a shared maritime zone with Libya in exchange for support from Turkey’s military. The deal, negotiated amid an ongoing dispute with Cyprus over rights to large natural gas deposits discovered in the eastern Mediterranean, would allow Turkey to impose a barrier that would disrupt a planned undersea natural gas pipeline passing from Israel to Greece through Cyprus.
2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict
Tensions flared between Armenia in mid-2020 over the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh. Turkey, showcasing its resolve in pursuing its regional interests, offered significant support for Azerbaijan’s armed forces, which overwhelmed Armenian forces in the zone of conflict. Russia, a guarantor for Armenian security, brokered a ceasefire in November that saw Armenian forces quit Nagorno-Karabakh on the agreement that the disputants allow Russian peacekeepers to patrol the disputed region for a minimum of five years. As part of the ceasefire, a corridor in southern Armenia also connected Azerbaijan proper to its southwestern exclave Nakhichevan, which borders Turkey; that connection incidentally guaranteed Turkey direct access to Azerbaijan and the Caspian Sea without passing through either Iran or Georgia.
2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine
Meanwhile, economic and defense ties between Turkey and Ukraine grew especially close during Erdoğan’s presidency. Apart from backing the potential accession of Ukraine into the EU and NATO—a military alliance understood as a counterweight in Europe to Russian military power—Turkey sold dozens of Bayraktar TB2 drones (unmanned aerial vehicles) to Ukraine and in February 2022 signed a free trade agreement with that country. Following a full-scale invasion of Russian forces into Ukraine later that same month, Turkey announced that it would restrict the movement of Russian warships into and out of the Black Sea, in accordance with the Montreux Convention (1936).
Erdoğan used the crisis to boost his leverage on the international stage. He initially held up the wartime accession of Finland and Sweden to NATO, citing their support for Kurdish rebels. His objections were dropped as those countries offered concessions, including agreements to extradite a number of Turkish citizens for trial in Turkey. In July Erdoğan positioned himself as a key mediator between Ukraine and Russia when he brokered a deal to allow the export of grain from Ukraine, the first signed agreement between the two countries since hostilities began.
Although Turkey continued to back Ukraine in the war, Erdoğan also fostered closer ties with Russia, despite its international isolation. Instead of participating in international sanctions against Pres. Vladimir Putin and his government, Turkey increased its exports to Russia and accommodated an influx of Russian tourists and migrants. The increased cash flow boosted Turkey’s ailing economy ahead of the 2023 presidential election.
Meanwhile, with Russia weighed down by war, Turkish-backed Azerbaijan broke its 2020 ceasefire agreement with Russian-backed Armenia and renewed its offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023. Russian forces were unwilling to intervene, allowing Azerbaijani forces to sweep into the region and assert control over it for the first time since Azerbaijan’s independence in 1991. The result was a major victory for Turkey’s geopolitical sphere of influence. It was surpassed in significance only by the toppling in 2024 of Bashar al-Assad in Syria—also made possible by Russia’s inability to intervene on Assad’s behalf.
In early 2024 Erdoğan offered to host a peace summit and serve as mediator to bring the Russia-Ukraine War to an end. Although the offer was not taken up that year, many observers saw Turkey to be in a unique position to fashion a compromise between the two countries.

articles.title: Central Asian railway plans open new trade opportunities for Pakistan's ports-INP - Independent News Pakistan
articles.summary: Central Asian railway plans open new trade opportunities for Pakistan's ports-INP  Independent News Pakistan
articles.full_text:
By Azam Tariq
Emerging railway connectivity plans linking Central Asia with Pakistan through Afghanistan could open new opportunities for regional trade and increase cargo movement through Karachi and Gwadar ports, potentially strengthening Pakistan’s position as a maritime gateway for landlocked Central Asian economies, according to experts.
The proposed Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway corridor, being explored under the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) project, could eventually handle up to 10 million tonnes of cargo annually towards Pakistan’s seaports, according to Kazakh authorities. However, the figure represents projected capacity rather than confirmed freight demand.
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates signed a memorandum on September 30 to examine the technical and economic feasibility of the proposed route. According to the Kazakh government, the parties plan to assess railway infrastructure, related logistics facilities and financing requirements, while also considering the formation of a working group to study the project's technical, economic and financial aspects.
The initiative complements the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway project, for which the three countries signed a framework agreement in July 2025 to conduct a joint feasibility study. Pakistan and Uzbekistan subsequently reaffirmed the Termiz-Kharlachi route and joint financing arrangements for the study.
Mujtaba Arshad, Research Associate at the Centre of Excellence for CPEC, Pakistan Institute of Development Economics, told Wealth Pakistan that the proposed railway could create new opportunities for Pakistan's logistics industry if transportation costs remained competitive and cargo movement was dependable.
He noted that railway connectivity would continue to rely on road transport because goods would still need to move between production centres, warehouses, railway terminals and ports.
According to Arshad, high fuel costs, complicated documentation requirements and uncertainty in cross-border cargo movement could weaken the commercial advantage of a geographically shorter route.
He said Pakistan needed to strengthen highways connecting major freight terminals with Karachi and Gwadar, improve customs clearance procedures and develop secure parking and cargo-handling facilities.
Closer coordination among railway authorities, port operators and road transporters would also be necessary to ensure that cargo moved efficiently across different transport networks, he added.
Usama Haider, President of the Karachi chapter of the All Pakistan Driver and Cleaner Association, told Wealth Pakistan that the proposed railway connections could create significant opportunities for Pakistan's transport and logistics industry, provided freight movement remained reliable and commercially competitive.
“A railway connection alone cannot guarantee increased trade unless there is sufficient freight demand and arrangements for uninterrupted cargo movement,” he said.
Haider explained that traders and logistics companies would assess the proposed corridor primarily on transportation costs, delivery times, border security and the reliability of cargo movement.
He said the integration of railway and road transport systems would be essential for making the corridor commercially viable. Even when long-distance cargo was transported by rail, trucks would remain necessary for moving goods between railway terminals, warehouses, industrial areas and seaports.
Efficient cargo handling, dependable road connections and competitive freight charges would therefore be as important as the railway infrastructure itself, he added.
The proposed corridor could provide Central Asian exporters with another route to international markets through Pakistan's ports, potentially expanding opportunities for freight handling, warehousing, transportation and related logistics services.
For Pakistan, greater transit trade could also support economic activity around major transport terminals and port facilities, although the scale of these benefits would depend on actual cargo volumes and the competitiveness of the route.
Haider identified security conditions in Afghanistan, unpredictable border closures and lengthy customs procedures as major challenges that could increase transportation costs and discourage freight operators.
He said Pakistan should prioritise closer coordination between railway authorities, highway operators and the ports of Karachi and Gwadar, alongside improvements in logistics terminals and cargo-handling facilities.
Digital customs procedures, predictable transit rules and shorter clearance times could further improve the corridor's competitiveness by reducing delays at borders and freight terminals, he added.
The growing interest in railway connections through Afghanistan reflects Central Asian economies' efforts to diversify access to international markets and strengthen regional trade connectivity.
For Pakistan, these initiatives offer an opportunity to expand its role in regional transit trade by combining maritime access with railway and road infrastructure.
However, the proposed Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan corridor remains at the study stage, and its eventual commercial impact will depend on financing, infrastructure development, security conditions and reliable cross-border arrangements.
If Pakistan can combine improved railway connectivity with efficient ports, predictable border management and integrated road logistics, Karachi and Gwadar could attract a larger share of Central Asian cargo traffic.
The longer-term opportunity lies in transforming proposed regional transport connections into commercially viable freight corridors that support trade, investment and economic cooperation across Central and South Asia.

articles.title: Moscow forum calls for restoration of diplomatic ties between Georgia and Russia - OC Media
articles.summary: Moscow forum calls for restoration of diplomatic ties between Georgia and Russia  OC Media
articles.full_text:
Participants at a forum in Moscow have proposed establishing a Russian-Georgian university, promoting the Russian language in Georgia, and restoring religious services at Georgia’s Lomisi Church, as part of a broader initiative to restore diplomatic relations between the two countries.
Georgia and Russia have had no diplomatic relations since the 2008 August War, but maintain trade and economic relations.
The forum took place on Wednesday, a week after Georgia’s government appointed First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia after a yearlong vacancy. His mandate also includes the peaceful resolution of the conflict with Russia.
A survey conducted by CRRC Georgia and the National Democratic Institute (NDI) in October 2023 found that roughly a quarter of respondents supported deepening economic ties with Russia, while a similar share favoured limiting them. Meanwhile, 34% said relations should remain as they were. Other polls taken around the same time indicated that a strong majority (77%) of respondents viewed Russia as Georgia’s primary political threat.
Following the forum, the Russian Interests Section at the Swiss Embassy in Georgia published a statement, emphasising that the event’s main goal was ‘to promote the restoration of diplomatic relations between the countries’.
The document further called on Russian President Vladimir Putin and the Georgian government to support closer bilateral ties.
The event in Moscow was attended by Russian Foreign Ministry official Vasily Gavrilov (not to be confused with Russian MP Sergei Gavrilov, associated with the 2019 ‘Gavrilov’s Night’ protest), and several Georgian figures associated with pro-Russian initiatives, including Otar Romanov-Phartskhaladze, a former Georgian prosecutor general wanted by Georgian authorities and sanctioned by the US and UK.
During the forum, a foundation called ‘Unity of Russians and Georgians’ was created. Its co-founders include Phartskhaladze, Moscow-based businessperson Mamuka Pipia, and Davit Tsetskhladze, head of the Russian-Georgian Business Council.
Shortly after its establishment, a separate resolution was signed that proposed expanding the foundation’s activities, establishing a public supervisory board involving representatives of science, culture, education, and business, and preparing an initial action plan to implement the proposals.
Speaking at the forum, Pipia, who is also the international secretary of the Georgian pro-Russian Solidarity for Peace party, said the initiative aimed to help restore diplomatic relations between Russia and Georgia and move from intentions to practical steps.
In turn, Gavrilov said improving relations between Russia and Georgia was in the interests of both countries.
‘We see Georgia not as a launchpad against anyone, nor as a chessboard for risky geopolitical games, but as a place for human contacts, trade corridors, tourist routes, and energy projects. And it is encouraging that today the voices of friendship are much louder than the voices of discord’, Gavrilov said.
The Lomisi Church itself mentioned in the resolution has had its own share of controversy. It is located in Kirbali, near the Georgian-Ossetian separation line, in territory under Russian control. In November 2023, Georgian citizen Tamaz Ginturi was fatally shot there, while another Georgian citizen was captured by Russian border guards in South Ossetia, reportedly while trying to reach a disputed church.

articles.title: BRI Projects Gain Pace In Central Asia - The Rising Nepal
articles.summary: BRI Projects Gain Pace In Central Asia  The Rising Nepal
articles.full_text:
Since ancient times—specifically from the 2nd century BC—the "Great Silk Road" and the numerous caravans traveling along it, passing through thousands of cities and settlements, connected Asia and Europe through trade, economic, cultural, and scientific ties. This route played a pivotal role in the development and prosperity of many cities and empires across Asia and Europe. Historically, Central Asia gravitated toward China; the Silk Road and its caravans traversed this region, and the "Celestial Empire" viewed Central Asia as an immediate belt surrounding its core—the Chinese empire itself.
In 2013, in Astana, Chinese President Xi Jinping first introduced the concept of a 21st-century "Silk Road Economic Belt." President Xi remarked at the time: "As I stand here today and look back at history, I can almost hear the ringing of camel bells echoing through the mountains and see thin plumes of smoke rising above the desert." The choice of Astana in 2013 for Xi’s statement highlighted the strategic role of Central Asia as a transit hub between East and West. Xi proposed an innovative model of cooperation based on five key principles (the "five connectivities"): policy coordination, a unified infrastructure network, trade facilitation, monetary and financial flows and people-to-people diplomacy.
Overall policy
Beijing’s overall policy regarding Central Asia and the "Middle Corridor" of the Belt and Road Initiative—a region of strategic importance for China’s military and energy security—is significant. There have been geopolitical developments behind choosing the “Middle Corridor,” as it is emerging as a key hub for economic growth and investment, enabling the region to reclaim its historical role as a transport link connecting the East and the West. China has established strategic partnerships with all Central Asian nations, grounded in the principles of good-neighborliness, mutual respect, equality, and trust. Today, camel caravans laden with silk, porcelain, and tea have been replaced by trucks and trains carrying steel, electric vehicles, machinery, modern technologies, and innovations. Just as in the past, the routes of these caravans traverse deserts, mountains, plains, steppes, and seas, bringing together a diverse array of peoples and cultures. China is the largest trading partner for every country in the region.
In 2025, the volume of trade between China and these countries reached $106.3 billion, an increase by 12 per cent compared to the previous year. Of this total, $49 billion accounts for trade with Kazakhstan, $18 billion with Uzbekistan, and $40.3 billion with Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. Exports from China to Central Asia reached a total of $71.2 billion (an 11 per cent year-on-year increase), driven primarily by machinery, electrical equipment, and high-tech products. China’s imports from Central Asia totaled $35.1 billion (a 14 per cent increase). Regarding foreign direct investment, Chinese capital—whether state-owned, private, or mixed—currently accounts for over 65 per cent of total foreign investment. The primary recipients of Chinese investment in the region are Kazakhstan (approximately 35 per cent), Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Kyrgyzstan.
A vast number of infrastructure projects, including the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan (CKU) railway line, a key project currently under construction (southern route), "Khorgos – Eastern Gate": a major logistics centre on the border between China and Kazakhstan that facilitates the transshipment of cargo, and the Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline: an energy artery consisting of four lines (lines A, B, C, and the planned line D) for the transport of natural gas from Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan to China. This cooperation encompasses the construction of cross-border cables and networks, satellite stations, data centres, and other components of digital infrastructure, as well as the exchange of technology and expertise within the digital sphere.
Currently, approximately 84 projects under the "Digital Silk Road" are being implemented or planned in Central Asia. Of these, 30 are located in Kazakhstan and 26 in Uzbekistan. Ten projects each are underway in Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, with a primary focus on "smart city" initiatives and the upgrading of telecommunications networks. Eight projects are in progress in Turkmenistan, focusing mainly on the laying of fibre-optic cables along the bed of the Caspian Sea.
Important countries
Turkmenistan is one of the most important energy suppliers to the PRC; Kazakhstan serves as a key financial hub for the "Belt and Road" initiative outside of China; Uzbekistan has chosen the PRC as its primary strategic partner in the military-technical sphere; and Georgia is the only state in the Caucasus (and one of the few in Europe, alongside Switzerland and Serbia) to have a free trade agreement with the PRC. Amidst radical geopolitical shifts that are reshaping perceptions of the "balance of power" and the "balance of threats," security cooperation between China and the countries of Central Asia has taken on particular significance.
China has a fundamental interest in maintaining stability in Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Kazakhstan—countries that border its Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region—and in preventing any attempts to destabilise the region. Relations between China and the Central Asian countries will continue to develop rapidly in the near future. China’s overall policy toward Central Asia—implemented through the BRI, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), and military-technical cooperation—aims to transform the region into a prosperous and stable zone within China’s sphere of influence.
(The author is a researcher and PhD candidate at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration.)

articles.title: Opinion: A Deeper Understanding of Transshipment - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Opinion: A Deeper Understanding of Transshipment  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The White House recently issued a report on the transshipment of goods. It focuses on allegations that some countries with lower tariffs seek to evade U.S. tariffs on China by exporting goods that are really produced in China and only slightly modified, if at all, before further export to the U.S.
The report groups more than 40 countries in what it terms a “shadow transshipment network” into three different categories based on how much it estimates the risk of transshipment and the integration of the economy into supply chains involving China. The first tier, mostly advanced countries, are larger economies where transshipment can show up in otherwise “broadly legitimate” trade. The second tier are a few larger developing countries, which have close links with the Chinese economy. The third tier the report terms “small, opportunistic Chinese targets” with “specific weak-link advantages” that increase transshipment risk.
To be clear, transshipment is a risk in some economies. There is also legitimate transshipment (for instance, through normal supply chains and logistics channels) and illegal transshipment (where an exporter files a false certification as to the origin, character, or value of goods). False certifications are punishable by civil and criminal penalties in the U.S. and in most other countries. The World Customs Organization also has international standards on transshipment.
So there are reasons to be vigilant about the risk of illegal transshipment. But to see why the report also misses the mark, consider the example of a country increasingly important to the U.S. with a fast-growing economy. To top it off, the country borders China. It’s Kazakhstan.
First, the report is wrong to call Kazakhstan “small.” It’s 49th in the world by GDP – quite an accomplishment for a country which was formerly part of the Soviet Union.
Second, to term Kazakhstan an “opportunistic Chinese target” is simply not accurate. There is strong trade and investment between China and Kazakhstan, as one would expect from large neighboring countries. And Kazakhstan, particularly at its Khorgos border cooperation center, plays a vital role in the rapidly growing Middle Corridor of trade between China and Europe.
But this is legitimate transshipment of goods, and it is deeply unfair to suggest that Kazakhstan may not be fulfilling its duties. Let’s also not forget why the Middle Corridor is growing: because the West sought another route for Chinese goods after the Russian invasion of Ukraine made shipment through Russia impractical or subject to sanctions.
Kazakhstan is a regional and even global leader in digitalization of both tax and Customs systems. The “smart border” policy is a success in facilitating legal trade while maintaining vigilance and security: in the first half of 2026, about 60% of declarations of goods were automatic, and 80% of transit declarations were completed without the need for Customs control forms. Deepening digital exchange protocols with regional partners including China, Uzbekistan, and Azerbaijan will speed legal trade even further.
Digitalization builds honest systems, free from corruption – and by definition lowering the risk of transshipment. Kazakhstan should be commended for this work, not lumped in with other countries that have not made similar investments in digitizing legitimate trade flows.
Most relevant, however, is the growing importance of U.S.-Kazakhstan trade. The U.S. exports a wide variety of products – turbines, aircraft, prescription drugs, agricultural machinery, and other goods as well as services such as software. Imports are concentrated in commodities including petroleum, chemicals, uranium, silver, ferroalloys, and titanium.
Faced with growing needs to find critical minerals, the U.S. has turned to Kazakhstan and other sources precisely to avoid overdependence on China. The U.S. and Kazakhstan have a critical minerals agreement precisely for this purpose. Again, all this should be commended rather than regarded with suspicion. In fact, imports from Kazakhstan are so vital to the U.S. that most are exempt from U.S. tariffs, because the U.S. recognizes that tariffs would hurt supplies of minerals the country needs.
More to the point, these goods have an exceptionally low risk of transshipment. The U.S. has invested in Kazakhstan’s oil and gas industry since the early 1990s and is well founded there. Oil would not be mislabeled as Chinese – it would make no sense to ship oil through a pipeline and then export via the Caspian Sea when Kazakhstan can fill those pipelines and tankers itself. And no one would send truckloads or boxcars of uranium and ferroalloys from China to Kazakhstan simply to avoid tariffs; that would be uneconomic.
The types of goods about which the report worries are typically finished manufactured goods (for instance, solar panels or auto parts) that might have originated in China and then been only “lightly” processed in another country. Not the kinds of goods that Kazakhstan exports, for which it also receives high-value U.S. goods in a growing trade relationship.
If there is a concern about Chinese investment in Kazakhstan and other countries, then the solution is to increase U.S. investment in natural resources and a wide variety of other economic sectors, from retail to light manufacturing. Ending the annual Jackson-Vanik certification 35 years after the end of the Soviet Union would help grow trade, too – Kazakhstan has free emigration policies and a thriving if small Jewish community. That Amendment has served its purpose and should be ended through the U.S.-Kazakhstan Trade Modernization Act.
The report therefore paints with too broad a brush. That metaphor works in another way as well: a paintbrush is small, portable, and generally inexpensive – the type of good for which a major difference in tariffs has a significant impact on competitiveness. But not uranium or iron alloys or titanium. In addressing serious risks to trade such as transshipment, it’s important to be precise – and to remember which of America’s friends are already taking the actions America seeks.

articles.title: India and Kazakhstan: A Partnership that Bridges Regions - NatStrat
articles.summary: India and Kazakhstan: A Partnership that Bridges Regions  NatStrat
articles.full_text:
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of BRICS Summit in New Delhi| DD News
India and Kazakhstan are not direct neighbours in the conventional geographical sense. However, geography should not determine the relationship. In the twenty-first century, countries are connected not only by borders, but by corridors, supply chains, technologies, investment, knowledge, people and ideas. The strategic task before India and Kazakhstan, therefore, is to turn geographical distance into connectivity, political goodwill into economic partnerships, and historical ties into a modern strategic relationship.
India- Kazakhstan Relationship: An Overview
The India–Kazakhstan Strategic Dialogue 2026 held on 24 September in Astana took place at a time when the bilateral relationship between the two countries has acquired a new degree of strategic relevance.
The timing could not be more appropriate, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the margins of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 13 September, 2026. The two leaders reviewed a remarkably broad agenda, from trade, energy, and connectivity to critical minerals, emerging technologies, security, and people-to-people ties, and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership between our countries.
While the two countries are now cooperating closely, the next step forward is to explore ways to make this strategic partnership more consequential. This is particularly important as we are living through a period in which the international environment is changing faster than many of the institutions and established patterns of cooperation. The global economy is becoming more fragmented. Supply chains are being reassessed, and connectivity is acquiring a strategic dimension. Energy security and critical minerals are moving higher on national agendas. At the same time, digital technologies, artificial intelligence and new forms of economic interdependence are reshaping the meaning of national competitiveness.
For countries such as India and Kazakhstan, these changes present not only challenges but also new opportunities. India is one of the world’s major economic, technological and demographic centres, with an increasingly important role in shaping the global agenda. Kazakhstan, meanwhile, occupies a distinctive position at the intersection of Europe, Asia, Russia, China and the broader Middle East, while possessing substantial energy and mineral resources and an increasingly important role in Eurasian connectivity.
India and Kazakhstan have different geographical positions, but in some respects they complement each other. This geographical diversity provides a foundation for a partnership that extends beyond bilateral engagement, making both countries as a bridge between regions.
Kazakhstan is India’s largest trade and investment partner in Central Asia. The two countries have also developed a substantial institutional architecture for cooperation, including the Inter-Governmental Commission and a number of joint working groups covering trade, transport and logistics, hydrocarbons, information technology, space, defence and other areas. However, institutions and political goodwill constitute only part of the equation.
An interesting paradox marks the relationship. Politically, India and Kazakhstan have developed a strong level of mutual trust. Economically, though, the relationship remains considerably smaller than its potential. Kazakhstan’s official figures put bilateral trade at about USD 923 million in 2025, while Indian and Kazakh officials have repeatedly spoken about the possibility of expanding trade towards USD 3 billion.
This gap between political potential and economic reality should be one of the central questions of the discussion among the policymakers. Although trade figures alone do not define the quality of a relationship, a genuinely strategic partnership ultimately requires a sufficiently broad economic foundation.
Potential Areas of Cooperation
There are several areas where the next stage of cooperation between India and Kazakhstan could be particularly significant that need to be identified.
Connectivity
First and the most crucial one is connectivity. For decades, geographical distance between Central Asia and South Asia has been one of the structural constraints on the economic relations. This is precisely why initiatives such as the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the use of Chabahar Port deserve sustained attention. At the 4th India–Central Asia Dialogue in 2025, the participating countries specifically emphasised the importance of the INSTC and welcomed Kazakhstan’s efforts concerning its eastern branch. They also stressed the need to simplify transit procedures and make greater use of mechanisms such as the TIR (Transports Internationaux Routiers/ International Road Transport) Carnet.
Connectivity, however, should not be understood simply as building roads, railways or ports. Connectivity is ultimately about making economic interaction easier. It means predictable transit procedures, efficient customs, financial connectivity, digital platforms, direct air links and reliable business-to-business contacts. There has been some encouraging movement in this direction. In June this year, Kazakhstan and Gujarat discussed launching direct flights between Almaty and Ahmedabad, alongside cooperation in pharmaceuticals, agriculture and investment.
Economic Diversification
The second important area of cooperation is economic diversification. Energy will remain an important component of the bilateral relationship. Kazakhstan has long been an important partner for India in the nuclear-energy sphere, including uranium supplies.The future relationship, however, should not be defined by hydrocarbons and uranium alone.
There is a much broader agenda before us: critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and food processing, information technology, artificial intelligence, renewable energy, petrochemicals, logistics, healthcare and advanced manufacturing. India has itself identified many of these sectors as areas with substantial potential and recent bilateral discussions have highlighted critical minerals, digital technologies, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and renewable energy.
In other words, the question is not simply how much more can the two countries trade? It is also what can they produce together? That is a more strategic question.
Technology & Human Capital
The third dimension is technology and human capital. India’s experience in digital public infrastructure, IT, pharmaceuticals, space and technological innovation is highly relevant to Kazakhstan and to Central Asia more broadly.
At the 4th India–Central Asia Dialogue, India offered cooperation in developing digital public infrastructure, while the participants agreed to establish an India–Central Asia Digital Partnership Forum. Cooperation in science, technology, space and innovation was also identified as a priority. This is an area where the cooperation could become much more ambitious.
Kazakhstan does not need simply to import technologies from India. The two partners should also look for opportunities to co-develop solutions, establish joint research and innovation projects, and connect our technological ecosystems.
The same principle applies to education. The relationship between the two societies cannot be built entirely through governments and businesses. Universities, think tanks, young professionals, researchers and students play an increasingly important role.
A strategic relationship requires not only diplomatic mechanisms but also an intellectual infrastructure, people who understand each other’s societies, strategic cultures, economic models, and regional perspectives.
Multilateral Cooperation
It is also critical to highlight the importance of multilateral cooperation between India and Kazakhstan. The two interact with each other through the United Nations (UN), the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) and other international platforms.
Kazakhstan is now a BRICS Partner Country, while India holds the BRICS chairmanship in 2026. During the recent bilateral meeting in July, the two sides specifically discussed cooperation within BRICS, including trade and investment, connectivity, digitalisation, artificial intelligence, energy and sustainable development. This adds another layer to the bilateral relationship.
India–Kazakhstan Strategic Dialogue 2026 held on 24 September in Astana | Arman Aisultan/ Qazinform
Shared Principles & Interests
The two countries do not necessarily have identical positions on every international issue – nor should they. Though there is considerable scope for cooperation on principles that are important to both such as respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, a stronger voice for developing and middle powers, reform of global governance institutions, greater connectivity across Eurasia, and a more inclusive international economic system.
And perhaps this is one of the most important reasons for having a strategic dialogue rather than simply a business forum or a roundtable. While a business forum asks: Where are the opportunities? A strategic dialogue should also ask: What kind of regional and international environment do we want to help create?
India and Kazakhstan are both countries with strong interests in stability, sovereignty, connectivity and development. Both are also geographically located in regions where the interaction of major powers is becoming increasingly consequential. Therefore, the cooperation between them should not be viewed through a narrow bilateral lens.
A stronger India–Kazakhstan relationship can deepen connectivity between Central Asia and South Asia, diversify economic partnerships, and strengthen the resilience of the wider Eurasian space.

articles.title: Kazakhstan and Türkiye: Partners Across the Middle Corridor - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Kazakhstan and Türkiye: Partners Across the Middle Corridor  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
On October 28 in Ankara, Kazakhstani President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan held talks in a narrow format and then with their delegations. They met less than six months after chairing the sixth bilateral High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council in Astana on May 14, suggesting a more intensive phase of presidential engagement.
The agenda covered transport and logistics, energy, agriculture and investment. Erdoğan reaffirmed the ambition to raise bilateral trade to $15 billion. The Middle Corridor remains central to bilateral cooperation, alongside trade, energy production and corporate investment linking both countries.
Complementary Commercial Roles
The partnership supports cargo flows both westward to Europe and eastward from Türkiye. In May, KTZ Express and Pasifik Eurasia organized a train carrying 50 forty-foot containers of refrigerators from Izmir toward Chengxiang in China via Aktau and Altynkol. KTZ Express reported an 83-hour transit on the Aktau–Altynkol leg within Kazakhstan. The companies are developing eastbound backhaul, coordinating schedules and transit arrangements to balance cargo flows. Turkish exporters gain a route through Kazakhstan toward Chinese customers, while the operators seek cargo to sustain services in both directions.
Kazakhstan’s inland rail network and Türkiye’s connections to European markets give the two countries complementary roles along the corridor. After crossing the Caspian, the Middle Corridor offers shippers an overland continuation through Türkiye alongside maritime routes through Georgian Black Sea ports. KTZ Express also cooperates with Maersk on Black Sea logistics. Azerbaijan and Georgia connect the Kazakhstani and Turkish sections of this route. Ankara and Astana share an interest in attracting cargo through Türkiye within this network of alternative routes.
Kazakhstan’s inland rail investment supports the route toward Türkiye. According to the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank’s 2026 project appraisal, the second track on the Dostyk–Mointy line has been completed. A further project would construct a new Mointy–Kyzylzhar section, bypassing congestion in central Kazakhstan to improve corridor alignment and capacity. Farther west, rail services reach Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports, where cargo transfers to maritime transport. Added rail capacity benefits bilateral services insofar as ports and vessels can accommodate the resulting flows.
Connecting the Route
Azerbaijan’s ports and railways connect Kazakhstan’s Caspian services with routes through Georgia to Türkiye. Crossing between rail networks separated by sea requires coordination of trains, vessels, and port handling. Kazakhstan’s container traffic uses Aktau, while Kuryk handles rail and road-vehicle ferries serving Alat in Azerbaijan. Kazakhstan and Türkiye therefore need cooperation with Azerbaijan and the operators responsible for transferring cargo between rail and sea.
Work on the Georgian section of the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway was completed in 2026. In June, Türkiye’s Transport Ministry described the completion as a new operational stage for the line, which opened in 2017. The railway carries cargo arriving through Azerbaijan across Georgia into Türkiye. At the June ceremony, Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu emphasized regular cargo flows, operational coordination, and reliable service.
Türkiye’s rail improvements toward the Bulgarian border strengthen its European connection and extend the corridor’s commercial reach. The Çerkezköy–Kapıkule section opened in October as part of the wider Halkalı–Kapıkule project; other sections remained under construction. The EU contributed €275 million in grant financing, linking European–Turkish infrastructure cooperation with the route toward Central Asia.
KTZ Express reports that corridor partners have introduced a common train schedule and automated shipment-data exchange. Its October account described coordination between rail and maritime services, using information on rolling-stock locations and advance consignments. According to the operator, these measures have reduced waiting at transfer points and improved delivery predictability.
Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have also agreed to authorize an additional 6,000 electronic road permits for 2026 and move exclusively to electronic permits from 2027. This road-haulage reform addresses border documentation, while the rail–sea measures coordinate transfers between services. Together, they address the administrative and operational interruptions that can limit the benefits of additional infrastructure.
Trade and Reciprocal Investment
Türkiye is among Kazakhstan’s major export markets, alongside Italy, China and Russia. Preliminary January–August 2026 statistics put its share of Kazakhstani merchandise exports at 7.9%, while it supplied 2.1% of imports over the same period. The presidential trade target thus builds on existing bilateral commerce. Improved services can support bilateral trade and help operators attract transit cargo destined for third markets.
Türkiye’s Mediterranean outlet at Ceyhan gives Kazakhstan an additional export option as it seeks to expand Trans-Caspian oil transit. KazMunayGas, Kazakhstan’s national oil company, moved 1.3 million metric tons along the Aktau–Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan route in 2025; its agreement with Azerbaijan’s SOCAR envisions a phased increase to 2.2 million metric tons annually. Tankers carry the crude across the Caspian for onward transport through the pipeline to Ceyhan.
KazMunayGas attributed the 7% decline in 2025 to technical restrictions in the pipeline system. A study commissioned by Tengiz and Kashagan shareholders is examining a much larger Trans-Caspian oil route, with options envisioning up to 35 million metric tons annually. The operating route reaches the Mediterranean without crossing the Black Sea or passing through the Turkish Straits. The service diversifies Kazakhstan’s export options and sustains Türkiye’s transit role. The larger proposal remains under commercial examination.
Aksa Energy, a Turkish power producer, announced full commercial commissioning of its 264-megawatt combined heat and power plant in Kyzylorda on June 1, 2026. Its 15-year capacity agreement with Kazakhstan’s energy settlement institution establishes a lasting Turkish commercial presence in Kazakhstan’s domestic energy market. Pharmaceutical production reinforces these ties: Nobel AFF, the Kazakhstani business of Türkiye’s Nobel Pharmaceuticals, operates a manufacturing facility in Almaty. These operations tie Turkish companies to demand within Kazakhstan, extending the commercial relationship beyond the movement of transit cargo.
Kazakhstan’s Kaspi.kz, a payments and e-commerce group, expanded into Türkiye by acquiring a controlling stake in Hepsiburada for approximately $1.127 billion. The transaction closed on January 29, 2025. The acquisition gave Kaspi an established Turkish marketplace serving local consumers and merchants. The Turkic Investment Fund has committed up to $20 million to Almaty Airport, operated by Türkiye-based TAV, adding regional financing to these bilateral ties, with Azerbaijan participating alongside Kazakhstan and Türkiye. Kaspi’s investment in Türkiye complements Turkish production in Kazakhstan. Companies in both countries thus have a continuing commercial interest in access to the other’s domestic market.
A Framework for Further Cooperation
Transport services and investment support Ankara’s and Astana’s multivector policies by widening their choice of routes, markets and commercial partners. Companies develop the services and commit capital; governments can sustain these options by maintaining market access, reducing administrative obstacles and coordinating with partners along the route.
Cooperation extends beyond commerce. Kazakhstan coordinates the military-political dimension of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), with Türkiye as co-coordinator; their work includes professional exchanges and mediation seminars.
For transport and investment, the Kazakhstan–Türkiye Council gives the presidents a forum for setting joint priorities. The Organization of Turkic States provides a multilateral setting, while the trilateral ministerial mechanism with Azerbaijan addresses their transport connections. Ankara and Astana can use their bilateral and transport forums to address obstacles requiring government decisions or coordination with other corridor partners.

articles.full_text:
Progress, Constraints, and Pathways Forward					
						
				 
		
This article examines U.S.-Vietnam semiconductor relations since 2023, arguing that despite alignment under the two states’ comprehensive strategic partnership (CSP), cooperation has yet to produce meaningful structural upgrading of Vietnam’s position in the global semiconductor value chain.
Executive Summary
MAIN ARGUMENT
The 2023 U.S.-Vietnam CSP marked a major upgrade in bilateral relations, with semiconductors identified as a central pillar of future cooperation. Yet progress to date has fallen short of initial expectations. This gap stems from two interacting factors. First, despite the upgrade, the U.S. has maintained a cautious approach toward Vietnam with policy incoherence and mixed signals that undermine momentum for deepening high-tech collaboration. This landscape has been further complicated by foreign and trade policy shifts under the Trump administration that have disrupted key cooperation mechanisms and increased uncertainty for U.S. firms. Second, and more fundamentally, Vietnam’s domestic ecosystem continues to face structural constraints, including inadequate infrastructure, workforce shortages, and constraints in the business environment. These limitations weaken Vietnam’s ability to attract and sustain high-value semiconductor cooperation. The CSP provides an important political framework but achieving its semiconductor ambitions will depend on credible policy support, firm-level confidence, and Vietnam’s capacity to address domestic bottlenecks.
POLICY IMPLICATIONS
- Vietnam should prioritize domestic capacity building as this remains the major challenge for deeper cooperation in the semiconductor sector. Without stronger infrastructure, a deeper talent pool, and a more predictable business environment, Vietnam will struggle to attract high-value and high-tech investment. Deepening engagement with U.S. firms and academic institutions is also crucial to anchor cooperation at the market level.
- The U.S. should align its policy tools with the strategic logic of the CSP. The continuation of Vietnam’s nonmarket economy status, restrictive export-controls, and high tariff pressures send mixed signals, weakening business confidence and limiting the momentum created by upgrading the partnership.
- Both sides should prioritize advanced packaging and workforce development as practical areas of cooperation. These areas match Vietnam’s current comparative advantages while supporting U.S. supply chain diversification, allowing cooperation to move gradually from low-value manufacturing toward more knowledge-intensive semiconductor activities.

Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan and Indonesia are exploring opportunities to expand bilateral trade and implement joint investment projects in agricultural processing. The issues were discussed by Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev and Indonesia’s Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan.
Bilateral trade increased by 82% in 2025, exceeding US$150 million. Khodjaev said further growth could be achieved by expanding the range of traded goods and increasing the participation of companies from both countries in joint projects.

To strengthen bilateral cooperation, Uzbekistan proposed resuming the work of the Intergovernmental Commission and organising a joint business forum.
Khodjaev said direct contacts between entrepreneurs, predictable business conditions and practical support for investment projects remain important prerequisites for advancing joint initiatives.

articles.title: Marriage Of Convenience: Russia And Iran Deepen Trade Ties, But Their Partnership Has Limits - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: Marriage Of Convenience: Russia And Iran Deepen Trade Ties, But Their Partnership Has Limits  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
It is said that politics makes strange bedfellows. Apparently international sanctions do too.
Russia and Iran, the world's two most-sanctioned nations, are deepening trade and financial ties to reduce their reliance on Western-dominated economic systems, a marriage of convenience through national currencies, direct banking links, and alternative transport routes.
This deepening economic cooperation is perhaps most visible in the Caspian Sea, where shipping activity between Russia and Iran has increased as Moscow's war in Ukraine and Middle East tensions disrupt established trade routes.
According to data from Castellum, a global risk adviser, Russia is now the most-sanctioned nation in the world with more than 5,000 international actions against it, followed by Iran with some 3,600 designations.
"Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Iran's destabilization have simultaneously spotlighted Eurasia's strategic importance while testing the limits of the region's historic alignments," Tina Dolbaia and Leah Kieff of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said recently.
Officially recorded bilateral trade between the two nations relies heavily on agricultural commodities: Russia exports grain and vegetable oils to Iran, while Tehran supplies fruits and vegetables in return.
Moscow's exports also encompass heavy industrial goods, including metals, timber, and machinery.
But beyond this transparent commercial exchange, the economic relationship contains a strategic military component.
According to the independent London-based maritime intelligence provider Lloyd's List Intelligence, the number of active Russian- and Iranian-flagged vessels operating in the Caspian rose 21 percent year on year in August.
The increase began in March, following US and Israeli strikes on Iran that started on February 28 and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. A US maritime blockade imposed in April further complicated Iranian shipping routes.
"The cargoes being transported are often difficult to identify," Lloyd's List reported, noting that trade data points to an increasing role for agricultural commodities.
Regional analyst Nitya Labh, who has written about the growth of Russia's and Iran's shadow fleets, points out that what began as an ad hoc practice involving a small handful of isolated nations has evolved into a massive, highly sophisticated global network.
"Today, estimates suggest the shadow fleet is over 1,300 vessels, accounting for at least one in every five oil tankers worldwide," Labh told RFE/RL.
Trade Has Grown Substantially
Russia's ambassador to Iran said in June that bilateral trade reached about $5.8 billion in 2025, up 21 percent from the previous year.
ProZerno, a Russian grain consultancy, reported that Iran imported 1.7 million tons of Russian wheat from July 2025 to January 2026, compared with 565,000 tons in the previous agricultural year.
Dolbaia, an associate fellow at CSIS, said agricultural products and foodstuffs dominate officially recorded trade. But the relationship also has a less transparent dimension involving military-related goods and efforts to limit exposure to Western sanctions.
Iran supplied Russia with attack drones early in Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but Russia has since localized and improved production, the expert said.
She added that there have been reports of Russia sending drone components to Iran via the Caspian Sea.
Alternative Payments
The two countries are also trying to make payments without relying on Western financial channels.
They have expanded settlement in rubles and rials and connected their respective interbank financial messaging systems, allowing banks to communicate allowing banks to communicate without using SWIFT, the international network banks use to exchange payment instructions.
A CSIS report co-authored by Dolbaia in April identified the International North-South Transport Corridor as a central element of that strategy.
The planned road, rail, and maritime network would connect Russia with Iran and extend toward the Persian Gulf and India through the South Caucasus and Central Asia, although major infrastructure and geopolitical obstacles remain.
More Trade, Harder To Track
Lloyd's List Intelligence found that the number of active general cargo ships on the Caspian route rose from 105 in February to 215 in August. The segment recorded a 36 percent year-on-year increase in carrying capacity, according to the report.
But the corridor cannot easily absorb the volume of trade handled by major maritime routes.
Ships are constrained by the Volga-Don river system, shallow water, declining water levels, limited port capacity, and rail bottlenecks.
Tanker activity has increased from a very low base. Three Russian-flagged crude-oil tankers were recorded on the route in August.
Lloyd's List said all three switched off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals as they approached Russian and Iranian ports, then reappeared during transit, obscuring the visibility of their cargo movements.
Ships are not required to keep AIS switched on in all circumstances, making activity in the Caspian difficult to track.
The CSIS researchers argue that sanctions evasion is one of the drivers behind the countries' efforts to develop alternative trade infrastructure. But the existence of a new route, or a vessel going dark on its tracking system, does not by itself prove that a specific shipment is illicit.
Allegations of military transfers through the Caspian have added to scrutiny.
Kyiv has accused Moscow of using the route to funnel military equipment.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported that Ukraine targeted several sanctioned cargo vessels in the sea following assessments that they were transporting military cargo.
ISW analysis also notes that the covert route has been utilized to shift sensitive defense assets, drone components, and ammunition.
Lloyd's List said the allegations remain unconfirmed, and neither government has publicly acknowledged such transfers.
While the European Union expanded its enforcement in 2026 by passing its 20th sanctions package to target shadow fleet owners, managers, and service providers, physical interdictions carry severe military risks, regional expert Labh warns.
Labh cited the risks of maritime enforcement, pointing to a May 2025 incident in which a Russian Su-35 briefly entered Estonian airspace as Estonia attempted to stop a suspected Russian shadow-fleet tanker.
In August 2026, Russia President Vladimir Putin separately threatened retaliation for Western seizures of Russian commercial vessels, calling them "piracy."
But despite the growing bilateral trade, Dolbaia cautioned against overstating what Iran can do for Russia.
"For Russia, cooperation with China is far more important to withstand Western sanctions effects than cooperation with Iran," she told RFE/RL, noting that China buys Russian energy and supplies components used in Russia's defense sector.
Russia's trade with China surpasses $200 billion annually, dwarfing the single-digit billions traded with Iran.

articles.title: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) | Map, Progress, Impact, & BRI - Britannica
articles.summary: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) | Map, Progress, Impact, & BRI  Britannica
articles.full_text:
,  massive bilateral project to improve infrastructure within Pakistan for better trade with China and to further integrate the countries of South Asia. It is part of the larger Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) to improve connectivity, trade, communication, and cooperation between the countries of Eurasia announced by China in 2013.
The project was launched on April 20, 2015, when Chinese Pres. Xi Jinping and Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif signed 51 agreements and memorandums of understanding valued at $46 billion. The goal of the CPEC is both to transform Pakistan’s economy—by modernizing its road, rail, air, and energy transportation systems—and to connect the deep-sea Pakistani ports of Gwadar and Karachi to the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in China and beyond by overland routes. (Xinjiang borders the countries of Mongolia, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and India, and the ancient Silk Road ran through its territory.) This aims to reduce the time and cost of transporting goods and energy such as natural gas to China by circumventing the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea. The initiative was also set to open several special economic zones (SEZs), modeled on similar zones in China that offer incentives for investment and are intended to spur rapid economic growth. The announcement of joint space and satellite initiatives between Pakistan and China, spurred by the CPEC, followed in 2016.
By the end of the 2010s, the program had achieved a number of successes for Pakistan, particularly in terms of infrastructure. Hundreds of miles of highways and railways had been completed. Pakistan’s capacity for electric power generation had also increased dramatically; although renewable energy made up only a fraction of the new energy projects, the country’s first solar power plant was inaugurated in May 2015. The Orange Line Metro Train system in Lahore, launched in October 2020 and the first of its kind in the country, was the most lauded urban project to come out of the early CPEC program.
But the CPEC initiatives proved to be a significant burden on Pakistan’s already strained balance of payments. Five years into the program, debt owed to China made up more than one-fourth of Pakistan’s total debt as it struggled to make its external payments. The economic impact of the global COVID-19 pandemic also slowed progress on CPEC projects, exacerbated Pakistan’s economic crisis, and left China hesitant to grant leniency on debt payments. Although the project gave a boost to job creation in Pakistan, promises that it would bolster Pakistan’s industrial sector and increase exports remained largely unrealized into the early 2020s. And even though the CPEC had expanded energy infrastructure, the costs for fossil fuel and upgrading an aging power grid led to continued power shortages and failures throughout the country. Furthermore, some construction, especially in the province of Balochistan, faced setbacks from violence by local militants who were opposed to the CPEC projects in their area.
