Net negative foreign direct investment (FDI) is an immediate red flag for international capital. While UNCTAD’s World Investment Report 2026 highlighted broader growth across Central Asia, Kazakhstan recorded a net FDI outflow of $861m in 2025.
However, Alibek Bakayev, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to the UK, offers a granular counternarrative.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.
For the UK, the more fundamental challenge remains diversification, with crude oil still accounting for more than 85% of British goods imports from Kazakhstan.
Speaking with Investment Monitor, the ambassador explains how Astana intends to channel British capital into various sectors.
IM: Can you describe the steps you are taking to increase UK capital flows into Kazakhstan and to strengthen the trade relationship between the two countries?
Bakayev: Since taking up my post, I have set a straightforward test for our economic diplomacy: how many credible projects progress from an initial conversation to financing and implementation.
The UK–Kazakhstan Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which entered into force on 3 June 2026, gives us a stronger framework across trade, investment, financial services, energy, transport and intellectual property.
It will also connect British investors, service companies and technologies directly with Kazakh project sponsors, the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and relevant decision-makers – to remain involved when investors encounter practical obstacles. Critical minerals provide the clearest example of this approach.
The latest UK data put bilateral trade in goods and services at approximately £2.6bn ($3.47bn) in the twelve months to the end of the first quarter of 2026. However, its composition is as important as its size: services account for more than three-quarters of UK exports to Kazakhstan, while crude oil represents more than 85% of UK goods imports from Kazakhstan.
While the relationship is substantial, it is still too concentrated. Diversifying it will require continued improvements in project preparation, procurement transparency, regulatory consistency and contract enforcement.
IM: Now that the UK-Kazakhstan Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement has been ratified, what does this change in practice for active investors on the ground?
Bakayev: The agreement is not a conventional free-trade agreement that removes tariffs overnight, nor does ratification automatically change every domestic licence or tax rule.
For investors committing capital to a mine, energy asset or infrastructure project for perhaps 15 or 20 years, greater certainty over the rules can be more valuable than a short-term incentive.
For British companies already operating in Kazakhstan, the agreement establishes a number of practical safeguards, subject to its terms and reservations. These include non-discriminatory treatment, protections for the transfer and repatriation of investment capital and profits, clearer licensing procedures, access to courts and administrative bodies, and greater regulatory transparency. Provisions on temporary entry should also make it easier for companies to deploy key personnel.
The real test will be implementation. Kazakhstan has chosen to bind itself to the standards set out in the agreement. Investors are entitled to judge us by how consistently we deliver them.
IM: The World Investment Report 2026 noted that while Central Asian FDI grew, Kazakhstan experienced a net FDI outflow of $861m in 2025. What steps are being taken to reverse this trend and support long-term inflows?
Bakayev: The $861m net outflow deserves attention, but it should not be read as $861m of cancelled projects or an economy-wide withdrawal by investors. FDI statistics include equity, reinvested earnings and intra-company debt. Kazakhstan’s negative balance in 2025 was overwhelmingly concentrated in mature oil and gas projects: that segment recorded approximately $6.3bn in net outflows as major investments, including the Tengiz expansion, moved from an intensive construction phase into production and capital repayment.
The National Bank’s gross-inflow measure rose by 14.4% to $20.5bn; manufacturing recorded a net inflow of around $1.7bn, while trade, finance and communications together attracted approximately $3.4bn. These measures are not interchangeable, but the underlying picture is clearly more nuanced than the headline.
We want to move beyond traditional resource extraction towards critical-minerals processing and recycling, power and grid infrastructure, Middle Corridor logistics, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and agrifood.
In London, we are engaging strategic investors, banks, asset managers, the London Stock Exchange Group and UK Export Finance (UKEF). UKEF is currently open for short- and long-term cover in Kazakhstan and indicates market-risk appetite of at least £5bn and local-currency financing available for medium- and long-term business. The task now is to convert that capacity into bankable transactions.
IM: Are any fiscal incentives, tax exemptions, or Special Economic Zone (SEZ) privileges being offered to British companies willing to invest in downstream processing?
Bakayev: Yes, but these are project-based incentives, not a UK-specific concession. Within an appropriate SEZ, income from qualifying activities can receive a 100% reduction in corporate income tax, alongside zero land and property taxes, zero-rated VAT on specified goods consumed in the zone and duty-free imports under the free-customs-zone procedure. For newer SEZ agreements, the principal tax-holiday periods are seven, 15 or 25 years, depending on project value.
Outside an SEZ, support is more project-specific. Under Kazakhstan’s 2026 investment and industrial-policy framework, qualifying projects may receive tax preferences for up to ten years, customs-duty or import-VAT relief on eligible equipment and inputs, in-kind grants such as land, and facilitation for specialist foreign labour.
For metals processing, a qualifying locally incorporated manufacturer may also seek priority access to domestic copper, aluminium or zinc. The current mechanism provides discounts against London Metal Exchange benchmarks of 5% for finished-goods production and 1% for intermediate products.
IM: Over 85% of UK goods imports from Kazakhstan are still crude oil. What specific strategies are you using to pitch non-resource sectors like ICT, green energy, or agriculture to British institutional investors?
Bakayev: The 85% figure is a fair warning that our merchandise trade remains too concentrated, and we should not try to explain it away.
Our approach in London is increasingly sector-specific and transaction-led: matching projects to investors with the appropriate mandate and ticket size, bringing sponsors, regulators and potential offtakers into the discussion, and following meetings with financial models, risk allocation and access to project data.
In renewable energy, we are presenting portfolios of wind, solar and storage assets supported by auctions and long-term power-purchase arrangements, with grid connection and currency exposure addressed from the outset.
In ICT, where Kazakhstan’s IT-service exports exceeded $1.1bn in 2025, we distinguish scalable software companies from data centres and digital infrastructure, which can fit long-duration infrastructure capital.
In agriculture, we are explicit that foreign investors cannot own or lease farmland. The opportunity instead lies in regenerative and climate-smart agriculture, water security, irrigation and water-efficiency technologies, food processing, carbon management and export logistics.
IM: Following the signing of the bilateral Critical Minerals Roadmap through 2027, how is it progressing?
Bakayev: The 2026–2027 roadmap covering geological exploration, processing and advanced technologies was signed in London in February 2026 and is still in its early implementation phase.
The near-term test is whether projects are passing the intermediate stages: access to better geological data, technical evaluation, bankable feasibility studies, processing solutions, long-term offtake and financing.
Our priority is not simply to extract more material, but to process it in Kazakhstan and connect it to resilient UK supply chains.
A tangible development came in July, when Kazakhstan’s Zhezkazganredmet and the UK’s Maritime House concluded a five-year rhenium offtake contract. Existing UK-Kazakh rhenium cooperation has already demonstrated a route into the Rolls-Royce supply chain.
IM: Are there any concrete exploration or extraction projects involving British businesses, such as Rio Tinto and Maritime House’s ongoing work, that are expected to break ground in the near term?
Bakayev: Rio Tinto’s Kazakhstan subsidiary has prepared an exploration programme for 2026–2031 covering the Kylshbay-1, Kylshbay-3 and Kylshbay-5 areas in the Moyynkum district of Zhambyl Region. Anglo American is also undertaking geological exploration activities in Kazakhstan. More broadly, we see an opportunity to bring additional UK companies into Kazakhstan’s copper sector.
IM: UK Department for Business and Trade data shows bilateral trade fell 2.8% year-on-year to the end of Q1 2026. What are the specific challenges to steady trade growth?
Bakayev: The 2.8% decline is measured in current prices. UK imports of Kazakh goods actually increased by 2.5%, while UK services exports to Kazakhstan remained broadly stable.
More than four-fifths of the £76m overall decline came from lower UK imports of services from Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan’s total goods trade also grew by 10.5% in the first quarter of 2026, so this is not principally a story of declining demand in our market.
The more fundamental challenge is that bilateral trade still lacks sufficient breadth and diversification. Kazakhs

articles.title: OTS Summit in Ankara: Turkey Looks to Strengthen Its Position as Central Asia Competes for Transit Routes - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: OTS Summit in Ankara: Turkey Looks to Strengthen Its Position as Central Asia Competes for Transit Routes  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived in Ankara on October 28, the day he delivered his annual State of the Nation Address, in which he announced plans to expand transport routes between China and Europe. On October 30, he will attend the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Turkey is preparing to take over the organization’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan, and Central Asian countries are seeking to accelerate freight transportation across the Caspian Sea.
Behind the shared rhetoric of Turkic unity lie specific economic interests. Kazakhstan is building railways and expanding its capacity to handle transit cargo from China. Azerbaijan is developing Caspian ports and transport infrastructure in the South Caucasus. Turkey wants to attract more freight moving between China and Europe through Central Asia, increasing its role as a transit hub.
A unified route looks much simpler on a political map than it does in the daily operations of transport companies. Between China and Europe, cargo crosses several borders, is transferred from trains to ships and back, undergoes customs clearance, and is subject to tariffs set by different operators.
Interest in alternative Eurasian transport routes has grown since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but the competition extends beyond freight. Ankara is looking to strengthen its political presence in Central Asia, where Russia and China retain considerable influence.
Summit events begin on October 29 with a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers, chaired by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. The nation’s presidents will meet on the following day. Participants are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, discuss investment, energy, digitalization, security, and appoint a new OTS secretary-general.
Tokayev and Kazakhstan’s Route to Europe
Tokayev’s visit to Turkey follows directly after his State of the Nation Address, much of which focused on infrastructure, including plans to open the 272-kilometer Bakhty–Ayagoz railway in 2027. The line is expected to add 20 million metric tons of annual freight capacity between Kazakhstan and China.
Tokayev also discussed construction of the Aral–Caspian highway. The project would establish a new transport connection between western and central Kazakhstan. According to government estimates, it could shorten certain freight routes between China and Europe by approximately 1,000 kilometers and reduce delivery times by up to three days.
Both projects are part of a broader effort to increase Kazakhstan’s revenue from international logistics. The country currently earns a substantial share of its transit revenue directly from freight transportation. Developing warehouses, terminals, processing facilities, and distribution centers could generate additional income.
Turkey occupies an important position in this network. An overland branch of the Middle Corridor passes through its territory en route to European markets; the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway connects Azerbaijan to Turkey’s rail network through Georgia.
On the sidelines of the Ankara summit, Turkish business associations plan to discuss border crossing operations, transportation costs, and the development of the Middle Corridor.
Transport geography, however, does not fit neatly within the OTS’s political boundaries. Georgia, through which the railway connecting Azerbaijan and Turkey passes, is not a member of the organization. China, which generates a substantial share of potential freight traffic, also remains outside it.
The Caspian section presents additional challenges. The capacity of the ports of Aktau, Kuryk, and Baku depends on the availability of vessels, weather conditions, and coordination of railway schedules. A delay along one section can eliminate the advantage of a shorter overland route.
Ankara Expands Its Influence, Astana Draws Boundaries
Turkey has steadily strengthened its ties with Central Asia through trade, education, defense cooperation, and infrastructure projects. The OTS brings these areas together within a permanent framework for high-level negotiations.
But the five member states do not share a unified foreign policy.
Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan belong to the Eurasian Economic Union alongside Russia, Belarus, and Armenia. Both countries are also members of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, while Turkey is a NATO member, and Uzbekistan maintains a policy of nonparticipation in military blocs.
Central Asian members also balance their ties with Turkey against relationships with China, Russia, and the European Union. Those outside partnerships complicate efforts to forge a common OTS foreign policy.
At the May summit in Turkestan, Tokayev rejected portraying the organization as a military or geopolitical alliance, emphasizing practical cooperation, a position analysts interpreted as evidence of differing visions within the OTS.
Turkey’s upcoming chairmanship brings these differences back into focus. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan wants to increase the OTS’s international standing, while its Central Asian members are pursuing closer cooperation without limiting their wider diplomatic and economic partnerships.
Uzbekistan Seeks Leadership of the Secretariat
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is set to visit Turkey on October 29–30, with Tashkent announcing plans for discussions covering trade, investment, transport logistics, tourism, environmental issues, and education.
Uzbekistan joined the OTS in 2019, after the organization’s other current members. According to Uzbekistan’s government, it has since proposed more than 85 initiatives across various areas.
The summit is expected to appoint a new secretary-general. Mehmet Seyfettin Erol, president of the Ankara Center for Crisis and Policy Studies (ANKASAM), anticipates an Uzbek representative taking the role for the first time. Such an appointment would strengthen Tashkent’s presence within the organization’s permanent institutions.
In his assessment, cooperation between Turkey and Uzbekistan could accelerate the organization’s work in trade, investment, energy, digitalization, and transportation.
Uzbekistan is seeking new transport links to international markets. As a landlocked country, it relies on neighboring states and transit partners to move goods westward.
However, Tashkent and Astana have competing transit interests. The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, could divert some freight from routes through Kazakhstan. Uzbekistan proposes linking the railway to the Middle Corridor, but the routes would still compete for cargo.
The OTS can help coordinate these projects, but its secretary-general cannot settle competing national priorities. Decisions on infrastructure financing and transport policy remain with national governments.
A Shared History Has Not Created a Common Market
The Organization of Turkic States was established in 2009 as the Cooperation Council of Turkic Speaking States and adopted its current name in 2021.
Its full members are Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey, and Uzbekistan. Hungary, Turkmenistan, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and the Economic Cooperation Organization have observer status. Northern Cyprus is recognized as an independent state only by Turkey, and its participation in the OTS has been a source of friction, according to analysts.
In recent years, the OTS has established several economic mechanisms, including the Turkic Investment Fund. Members are also expanding cooperation among customs authorities, transport operators, and business associations. But there is no common market within the organization. Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan follow the customs rules of the Eurasian Economic Union, while the other members operate under their own trade regimes and international agreements.
Yaşar Sarı, a professor at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University and director of the Heydar Aliyev Center for Eurasian Studies, considers strengthening existing institutions more important than expanding the OTS or attempting to form a new geopolitical bloc. In an interview with CASPIA Lab, he advocated developing economic integration, transport cooperation, and regional coordination.
The OTS can help finance projects and coordinate negotiations, but national governments retain control over transport policy. Its members also have commitments to partners outside the organization, limiting how far they can act together. Agreeing on a joint statement is easier than negotiating lower freight charges or shorter border delays across several countries.

articles.full_text:
Ambassador of Kazakhstan to Indonesia, Serzhan Abdykarimov, presents his remarks at the third meeting of the Kazakhstan-Indonesia Friendship Society by the Kazakhstani Embassy in Jakarta on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). ANTARA/Nabil Ihsan.
He said preparations for the visit were among the main objectives of Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Anis Matta's working visit to Kazakhstan last June, during which he met with several Kazakhstani officials.
"The Deputy Minister's visit to Kazakhstan is also preparing for the upcoming state visit of the President, His Excellency Prabowo Subianto, to Kazakhstan next year," Abdykarimov said at the third meeting of the Kazakhstan-Indonesia Friendship Society, hosted by the Kazakhstani Embassy in Jakarta on Wednesday.
Beyond preparations for Prabowo's visit, Matta also focused on strengthening ties between the two countries and identifying new opportunities for bilateral cooperation, the ambassador said.
The Kazakhstani government is also preparing a package of more than 20 bilateral agreements covering trade, investment, digitalization, tourism, education, and other sectors, Abdykarimov said.
Kazakhstan also expects a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin) and Kazakhstan's Chamber of Commerce to be signed during the visit.
"The MoU will establish an effective partnership and a bilateral business council," he added.
If the visit takes place as planned, it would mark the fourth meeting between Prabowo and Kazakhstani President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev since 2026. The two leaders have met three times over the past year on the sidelines of major international events: the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, the Board of Peace summit in Washington in February, and the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September.
Abdykarimov said bilateral trade currently stood at around US$250 million. Although the figure was encouraging, he said there was considerable room to expand trade between the two countries.
He expressed optimism that the free trade agreement between Indonesia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), signed last year, would significantly strengthen trade ties with Kazakhstan, an EAEU member.
The ambassador also highlighted opportunities to expand cooperation in trade and investment, transport and logistics, energy, mining, digitalization, education, tourism, and people-to-people exchanges.

articles.title: Uzbekistan–Turkey Strategic Partnership: President Mirziyoyev’s Working Visit And The 13th OTS Summit - OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Uzbekistan–Turkey Strategic Partnership: President Mirziyoyev’s Working Visit And The 13th OTS Summit - OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev arrived in Türkiye on 29 October for a working visit combining bilateral talks with President Erdoğan and participation in the 13th Organization of Turkic States Summit.
- The leaders signed five agreements covering a High-Level Business Support Council, expanded preferential trade, social security and border information exchange, as bilateral trade reached $3.1 billion in 2025 with a $5 billion target.
- Mirziyoyev also met major Turkish firms on projects in energy, mining and infrastructure and will attend the 30 October OTS summit, after which Türkiye will assume the organisation’s chairmanship.
President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev arrived in Türkiye on October 29 for a working visit at the invitation of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. The visit combines Uzbekistan’s participation in the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) with a bilateral agenda focused on trade, investment, transport, business cooperation and the further development of the comprehensive strategic partnership between Tashkent and Ankara.
Mirziyoyev arrived in Ankara together with his wife and was welcomed at Etimesgut Airport by Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz and other officials. The visit started with a meeting with Uzbek citizens living in Türkiye. Mirziyoyev spoke with compatriots about their lives, education and future plans, while emphasizing the importance of knowledge, science and continued connection with Uzbekistan. According to a 2025 report of the Turkish Interior Ministry, the number of Uzbeks officially registered with residence permits in Türkiye exceeded 58000 making it one of the top 10 largest foreign communities living in the country.
The president was then officially welcomed by Erdoğan at the Presidential Complex, where the two leaders held bilateral talks. The meeting focused on strengthening relations at the level of comprehensive strategic partnership, including political and diplomatic cooperation, trade and economic ties, and cultural and humanitarian relations. Both sides noted that bilateral trade and investment, the number of joint ventures and air connections have continued to grow in recent years.
Furthermore, five bilateral documents have been signed. The two presidents signed an agreement establishing a High-Level Business Support Council, creating a new mechanism for closer coordination with the business community. The sides also signed a protocol expanding the list of goods covered by the Preferential Trade Agreement, an intergovernmental agreement on social security together with an administrative agreement for its implementation, and an additional protocol updating the 2022 agreement on the advance exchange of information concerning goods and vehicles crossing the countries’ borders.
These agreements address several practical barriers to closer economic relations. Expanding preferential trade can provide businesses with access to a wider range of goods under more favorable conditions, while improved information exchange can make cross-border movement more efficient. The social security agreement is also important for citizens working or living in the two countries, as it establishes a framework for protecting their social rights. Meanwhile, the new High-Level Business Support Council is expected to provide an additional institutional channel for developing investment and joint projects. Bilateral trade reached $3.1 billion in 2025, and the two countries have set a target of $5 billion.
The talks also reflected the broader strategic direction of the partnership. Erdoğan emphasized that Türkiye intends to continue advancing cooperation with Uzbekistan in trade, investment, mining, transportation and the defense industry. The two presidents also discussed expanding the portfolio of promising projects, preparing for the next meeting of the Joint Intergovernmental Commission and continuing practical cooperation in new areas. Erdoğan also invited Mirziyoyev to the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya in November.
Beyond the presidential talks, Mirziyoyev also met with representatives of major Turkish companies, including EKSIM Holding, Evyap Holding and OYAK. The discussions covered portfolio of projects, ranging from renewable energy, geology and mining to infrastructure, electric vehicle charging networks, food production, chemicals and construction. The meetings highlighted the growing role of Turkish private companies in Uzbekistan’s economic development, with a particular focus on new investment projects, localization of production and participation in infrastructure development.
On October 30, Mirziyoyev is scheduled to take part in the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Ankara, held under the theme “The Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.” The summit will focus on expanding cooperation in trade, investment, transport and logistics, culture, tourism, ecology and education, while the leaders are also expected to exchange views on regional and international issues. The meeting is expected to conclude with the Ankara Declaration and a package of decisions and documents, while Türkiye will assume the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan, giving Ankara’s summit an additional institutional significance.

Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan and Hong Kong have discussed expanding investment and trade cooperation, including establishing joint ventures, helping companies enter new markets and strengthening business ties.
Jamil Maksudi, adviser to the chairman of Uzbekistan's Chamber of Commerce and Industry, held talks with a Hong Kong business delegation led by Fang Zikang, deputy chairman of the Hong Kong United Trade and Industry Association.
The delegation included executives from trade and industry associations in Hong Kong and Guangdong province, as well as representatives of companies operating in investment, high technology and food services.
According to the delegation's head, the federation, which brings together more than 10,000 enterprises, intends to expand its presence in Central Asia under the Belt and Road Initiative, with Uzbekistan identified as one of its priority destinations.
Hong Kong business representatives expressed interest in establishing companies in Uzbekistan and investing in the hospitality, food service and education sectors.
A company specialising in drone manufacturing is also considering establishing an assembly facility in Uzbekistan using semi-knocked-down (SKD) components.
Another major topic was the possibility of major Uzbek companies and banks gaining access to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
To explore these opportunities, the participants proposed organising a business mission to Hong Kong involving representatives of Uzbekistan's financial sector and major enterprises.
The discussions also covered the establishment of a joint electronic business-to-business (B2B) platform for companies from Uzbekistan, Hong Kong and China.
Hong Kong business representatives said they were prepared to create dedicated sections for Uzbek enterprises on existing trading platforms in Hong Kong and Xi'an.
The initiative is intended to provide additional channels for business cooperation and help Uzbek companies access new markets.
The Hong Kong delegation was also invited to participate in the international forum "New Uzbekistan: Crossroads of Global Markets", scheduled for 29 November to 5 December 2026.
Following the meeting, the parties agreed to establish a joint working group and continue exchanging business delegations.
Uzbekistan's Chamber of Commerce and Industry confirmed its readiness to assist Hong Kong companies in identifying local partners and establishing contacts with relevant government agencies.
The proposed initiatives are aimed at expanding bilateral business ties, attracting investment and creating additional opportunities for companies seeking to operate in Uzbekistan and international markets.

articles.title: India–Uzbekistan Comprehensive Strategic Partnership: Deepening Cooperation and Unlocking New Opportunities - UzDaily
articles.summary: India–Uzbekistan Comprehensive Strategic Partnership: Deepening Cooperation and Unlocking New Opportunities  UzDaily
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s State Visit to Uzbekistan on 29-30 August 2026 has injected fresh momentum to an expanding relationship rooted in centuries of historical and cultural connections. This was the fourth visit of Prime Minister Modi to Uzbekistan with the previous being in 2015 (bilateral), 2016 and 2022 (SCO Summits).
With a population of approximately 37 million with young demographics and the only one sharing borders with all four other Central Asian countries, and also Afghanistan, Uzbekistan is emerging as an important hub for regional commerce and diplomacy. For Uzbekistan, partnership with India offers access to a major economy, new sources of investment and opportunities to diversify its international economic relationships. Uzbekistan’s many achievements since achieving independence are impressive and it has become one of the most dynamic and fast-growing economy in the region. India is the fastest growing major economy in the world.
One of the key outcomes of the PM Modi’s visit has been the elevation of bilateral relations from a ‘Strategic Partnership’ forged in 2011 to a ‘Comprehensive Strategic Partnership’ in 2026 signalling a commitment to move beyond traditional diplomacy towards a more ambitious, multi-sectoral relationship.
Trade and investment has been identified as the key driver of the relationship. Between 2017 and 2025, the bilateral trade turnover increased fourfold, from US$ 324.9 million to US$1.3 billion. During PM’s visit, an ambitious target has been set to increase the bilateral trade to US$ 5 billion by 2030. Achieving this will require stronger business links, greater investments and the removal of non-tariff barriers. Uzbekistan has diversified its economy with manufacturing and other industries playing an increasingly important role and also offers opportunities in minerals, agriculture and improved access to Central Asian markets. India’s strengths in pharmaceuticals, engineering, information technology, healthcare and mining technology complement Uzbekistan’s development priorities creating opportunities for a mutually beneficial engagement. Although connectivity remains a significant challenge, innovative and determined approaches can help in strengthening cooperation. In order to realise the true potential of our bilateral relations, mechanisms have been set up at the level of foreign and trade ministers for supervision.
Critical minerals have emerged as an important area of cooperation. With the signing of agreement on cooperation in the area of geology and mineral resources, both countries have affirmed interest in exploring opportunities in geological surveys, mining, mineral processing and the development of resilient supply chains. For India, diversified sources of strategically important minerals can support manufacturing, electronics and renewable energy while for Uzbekistan, cooperation with Indian companies could bring investment, technical expertise and opportunities to develop higher-value industries.
Energy cooperation is equally significant. Uzbekistan is an established supplier of uranium to India, and continuation of the supply arrangement is important to India’s long-term nuclear energy ambitions. There are also opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy and related technologies. Uzbekistan’s experience in coal gasification can also be useful for India’s own push to derive clean energy.
Digital payments is an area which has witnessed significant progress. The commercial agreement signed between NPCI International Payments Ltd (NIPL) with National Interbank Processing Centre JSC (NIPC), Uzbekistan will link the Indian UPI Apps with Uzbekistan’s national QR payment infrastructure making transactions more convenient and providing a boost to tourism and retail businesses. Collaboration in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, startups and skill development would deepen technological ties and encourage innovation while creating opportunities for young professionals.
Our increasing defence cooperation adds an important dimension of trust and security to the relationship. Both our countries have shared interest in counterterrorism and regional stability. The joint military exercise, Dustlik, and institutional engagement in counter terrorism has enhanced professional exchanges and operational cooperation.
Education is another enduring pillar between the two countries. An agreement on cooperation in the field of higher education and scientific research has been signed with a view to foster academic exchanges and partnerships. Our linguistic connections have influenced various aspect of our shared history and development. There is growing interest in India for learning Uzbek language. Eminent Indian Universities such as Jawaharlal Nehru University and Jamia Milia Islamia University offer Uzbek language programmes. Similarly, Hindi is also being taught at Tashkent State University of Oreintal Studies, University of World Economy and Diplomacy, Uzbekistan State World Languages University and Shastri School in Tashkent. With deepening ties between India and Uzbekistan, Hindi and Uzbek have become languages of opportunity. The institution of 100 annual Lal Bahadur Shastri Scholarships for Uzbek students learning Hindi reflects India’s deep desire to not only strengthen our linguistic linkages and enhance people-to-people interactions but also transition our youth into key contributors to our progress and development.
We also have Buddhist and Sufi connections. Our offer for conservation and restoration of ancient Buddhist sites of Fayaz Tepa and Kara Tepa in Termez is part of our effort to preserve and promote tangible cultural and spiritual connections with Uzbekistan.
Cooperation in healthcare and pharmaceuticals also offers significant scope to improve access to medicines, expand technical expertise and encourage local manufacturing. We have shared a long history of cooperation and exchanges in healthcare. Ibn Sina, one of the most eminent philosopher and physician from Bukhara, was aware of the principles of Ayurveda and his work was influenced by Indian medicinal knowledge and practices. With the signing of MoU on Cooperation in the areas of traditional medicine, we are looking at expanding our engagement in Ayurveda and wellness tourism.
With sustained commitment and practical cooperation, India and Uzbekistan are poised to transform their longstanding friendship into a modern strategic partnership that advances economic growth, strengthens regional stability and delivers lasting benefits to their people.
